newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Market still playing defense.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Market still playing defense.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will likely continue to play defense Friday ahead of a fresh batch of data as players remain wary after hawkish Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments this week, analysts said.

"Maybe we'll get some sort of stabilization, but really it doesn't look to me there is any particular reason why we should get a significant rally on Friday," said Paul Kasriel, chief domestic economist at Northern Trust.
"The market is going to continue to play defense ahead of the (February) employment report next week," he added.

Analysts said market sentiment shifted to a cautious mode after the first leg of Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday, when the Fed chief said he could not rule out higher rates as a pre-emptive strike against inflation.
"Greenspan appropriately put the focus back on growth and on the fact that the Fed has to be pre-emptive," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

"Greenspan is telling you that we're closer to a (monetary policy) tightening ... It seems more likely that you'll have events occurring that would force the Fed to move in May or later in the summer," Glassman added.
Glassman added, however, that "many people in the market think that the March (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting is still a live option."
The market will take in some important data on Friday, including the release of the revision for the fourth quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Wall Street economists in a Reuters survey said they expect, on average, GDP to be revised down to 4.1 percent growth in the fourth quarter from a previously reported 4.7 percent.
A lot of attention is expected to be placed on the price index component of the report, which is expected to stay unchanged at 1.8 percent.

The market will also take in a slew of fresh data at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. January existing home sales, the final February University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index and the February Chicago Purchasing Managers Index (PMI).
"I think the background music is still not good ... But there is always the potential for short-covering once you get through the numbers," said Jerry Zukowski, money market economist at PaineWeber.
Despite the recent strong selloff seen in the last two sessions, analysts said the short-end of the market still has not fully priced in a possible Fed tightening.

"I don't think the market, especially the short end, has really priced in a March tightening yet," Kasriel said. "They are starting though. They got more in today than they did two days ago," he added.
On Thursday, the Federal Reserve added temporary reserves to the banking system through overnight system repurchase agreements, when the federal funds were quoted at 5-1/4 percent.
Fed funds are seen opening at 5.31 percent on Friday, slightly above the Fed's 5.25 percent target.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 14/32 at 97-21/32 in late Thursday trade to yield 6.81 percent.
